title: Team Charter
description: The team charter that the team wrote together — versus the template the SM filled in alone. One page. Read once a quarter. Used as the reference when something feels off and nobody can name why. The discipline is not in writing it; it's in revisiting it.
empty_template_md:
# [Team name] — Team Charter
_Written [date] · last revisited [date] · next revisit [date]_

## Why this team exists
_One paragraph. The outcome this team is accountable for, in language a senior engineer in another team could understand._

## What we'll deliver in the next 90 days
_Three to five outcomes (not features). Specific. Dated._

## How we'll work together
_Working agreements. See sm-working-agreements playbook for the structure. Three to five items, agreed by the whole team._

## What we'll measure
_How we'll know we're succeeding. Three to five measures. Lagging is fine; we want signal, not theatre._

## Who's in the room and what each person brings
_Each team member: name, role, what they're great at, what's their stretch this quarter._

## What we don't do
_The boundaries. What this team is not responsible for. Saying no to the wrong work is half the job._

worked_examples.content_md:
# Customer Portal Team — Team Charter
_Written 22 March 2026 · last revisited 22 March 2026 · next revisit 22 June 2026_

## Why this team exists

We're replacing the legacy customer portal with a self-service experience for our top-12 B2B customers. By the end of this work, the portal team in CS will spend less time fielding password-reset calls and more time on relationship work that actually moves accounts forward.

## What we'll deliver in the next 90 days

- A working portal in production by 9 September that supports login + account management + three report types + password reset + admin console.
- A CS team that can hard-cutover the top-12 customers to the new portal on go-live day, with the workflow documented.
- An archived migration path for customer data older than 24 months, with a Phase-2 commitment about what we'll do with it.
- A measured reduction in CS-team-fielded password-reset tickets, from a current baseline of ~30/week.

## How we'll work together

- Standup at 10am, 15 minutes, problem-solving moved offline.
- Code review SLA: 24 hours, first response. Same-day for blocking PRs.
- Compliance review at week 7, not later. Any data-residency questions surface there.
- Naledi's QA work has a one-day buffer before any production deploy that touches payments.
- We work to the team's capacity, not the PO's wishlist. The PO and the SM hold this line together.

## What we'll measure

- Sprint goal achievement (target: 6 of 8 sprints land their goal fully).
- Deployment-to-staging cycle time (current: 2-3 days; target: <1 day).
- Impediment resolution median (current: 5 days; target: <4 days).
- Team-health survey: 'I can do my best work here' — scored monthly, anonymous.

## Who's in the room

- **Lewis Harding (Lead Dev):** great at platform-deep technical reasoning; stretch this quarter is mentoring Theo without solving Theo's problems for him.
- **Naledi Mokoena (QA Lead):** great at finding the regression nobody saw coming; stretch is owning the QA strategy for the bulk-import work in Phase 2.
- **Theo Park (Junior Dev / Design crossover):** great at design-engineering bridge work; stretch is owning a story end-to-end with no senior pairing.
- **Asha Bhatt (Senior Designer):** great at making complex flows feel simple; stretch is teaching the design language to engineers via component patterns.
- **Hari Quintero (PO, not on this team but adjacent):** brings stakeholder access; stretch is being in fewer planning meetings (delegating to the team).
- **[SM]:** brings the holding-the-space role; stretch is the platform-team transition conversation Adisa flagged for Q3.

## What we don't do

- We don't migrate customer data older than 24 months in this programme (Phase 2 candidate).
- We don't own customer-facing communications (that's CS via Janelle).
- We don't take on the self-service billing work — that sits with finance.
- We don't run prod outage response (SRE rotation handles that).

annotations.note: Why-this-team-exists in language understandable by a senior engineer in another team. Most charters fail the 'would my counterpart in another team understand this?' test. The discipline is plain English.
Outcomes, not features. 'Working portal' is a feature; 'CS spends less time fielding password resets' is an outcome. The team needs to see the impact of the work, not just the work.

The 'stretch this quarter' line per person is the most-skipped section and the most useful. It gives every team member something specific to grow into and gives the SM something specific to coach against.
What we don't do is the boundary the team can point to when scope creeps. Saying no to the wrong work is half the job — and having it written down makes the no much easier to defend.

common_mistakes: Charter written by the SM alone and presented to the team for approval. Wrong direction. The charter is the team's; the SM facilitates the writing of it.
Charter written in week 1 before the team has worked together enough to know how they want to work. Write a working charter in week 4 or 5; revisit it as a real charter at the quarter mark.
Outcomes confused with outputs. 'We will ship the portal' is an output. 'CS spends less time on password resets' is the outcome of the output. The charter wants outcomes.
What-we-don't-do section omitted. The team has no boundary to point to when the next opportunistic ask comes in. Always include it.
Charter filed and never re-read. Set a quarterly revisit date in the document itself. The first revisit is when the team learns whether the charter is real or theatre.
Charter that has nothing about the people in the room. The 'who's in the room' section makes the document a living team document, not a template. Skip it and you have a project brief, not a charter.
variant_patterns: Cross-functional team variant: 'who's in the room' grows to include adjacent roles (PO, designer, SRE liaison). Boundaries section becomes more important — what we own end-to-end vs. share.
Long-running team variant (team has existed for years): the 'why this team exists' section gets revisited annually. Often what was true two years ago no longer holds.
New team forming variant: the charter gets written in two passes — a draft in week 4, a real version in week 8. The first pass is the SM's; the second pass is the team's.
